passage:
Astrid told herself it was love. She checked Vera's phone only because people online could be dangerous. She kept Vera's bank card in the kitchen drawer because Vera was bad with money. She had steered her towards the grey coat instead of the red one, because red drew looks. And Vera's friends from the choir? Astrid simply mentioned how tired Vera always seemed after seeing them.
Tonight Vera asked, carefully, "Can I go to Mette's birthday on Friday?"
Can I. Astrid noticed the words. A year ago Vera sang solos, argued about books, cycled home at midnight.
"If you want," Astrid said, and watched Vera's shoulders stay tight, as if even a yes was a test.
Later, alone in the kitchen of the Oslo flat, Astrid opened the drawer and looked at the card. Under the word love she could hear something colder: if Vera needs me for everything, she can't leave.

qa.q: Where did Astrid keep Vera's bank card?
qa.a: She kept Vera's bank card in the kitchen drawer.

qa.q: What does Astrid feel underneath her idea of love?
qa.a: Astrid fears losing Vera; the colder thought is that if Vera needs her for everything, Vera can't leave.

qa.q: What turning point could Astrid act on after looking at the card?
qa.a: Astrid could hand back the card and stop checking the phone, and seek help from a counsellor for the fear of losing Vera, instead of tightening control.

qa.q: How has Vera's life changed over the year?
qa.a: Vera once sang solos and cycled home at midnight; now she asks permission to go to a birthday and stays tense even at a yes.

grounding: A woman controls Vera's phone, money, clothes and friends while calling it love, and glimpses the fear of losing power underneath.

passage:
The family counselling centre had a fish tank, and Ira watched the fish instead of Tenzin.
The counsellor had asked Tenzin to describe an ordinary day. Tenzin spoke slowly. "I send Ira a photo when I reach work. I share my location. Ira checks my expenses every Sunday. I don't wear the blue kurta any more, because Ira said it looked like I was trying to impress someone. I stopped the pottery class."
Ira's face burned. "I do all that because I worry. The city isn't safe. Money goes so fast."
"What would happen," the counsellor asked Ira gently, "if Tenzin didn't send the photo one day?"
Ira meant to say I'd be worried. What came out was, "I'd feel like I was losing her."
The room went very quiet. Tenzin looked at Ira for the first time that hour.

qa.q: What does Tenzin send Ira on reaching work?
qa.a: Tenzin sends Ira a photo on reaching work.

qa.q: What did Ira truly feel when asked about a missed photo?
qa.a: Ira felt afraid of losing Tenzin; the words "I'd feel like I was losing her" came out instead of "worried".

qa.q: What could Ira do after this honest moment in counselling?
qa.a: Ira could keep working with the counsellor on the fear itself and start giving Tenzin back choices, like the pottery class and privacy with money and location.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin to hear Ira's admission?
qa.a: Tenzin looks at Ira for the first time that hour, perhaps surprised, and maybe a little hopeful, to hear the fear named instead of excused as worry.

grounding: In counselling, Ira hears Tenzin describe a daily life shrunk by monitoring and rules, and admits it comes from fear of losing her, not only worry.
